title: Typesetting Machines and Printed Pictures
summary: A struggling actor found he could print from a flat stone using grease and water, and colorful posters soon covered city walls. Then clever machines learned to set type from a keyboard, casting whole lines of hot metal in seconds. And by turning photos into tiny dots, newspapers could finally print real photographs.

sections.heading: An Actor in Debt and a Slab of Stone
paragraphs: Our story begins not with an engineer but with an actor. Alois Senefelder was born on 6 November 1771 in Prague, where his father, also an actor, was performing at the time. The family lived in Munich, in Bavaria, and young Alois studied law before following his father onto the stage. He also wrote plays, and one of them was a success.

His next play was not. Printing it cost money, and Senefelder ended up in debt. Copying plays by hand was slow, and paying a printer was expensive, so he wondered whether he could print his own writing cheaply. He tried etching letters into copper plates, the way artists made engravings. But copper was costly, and writing backwards into it took a lot of practice.

For practice, he used slabs of a fine, smooth limestone that came from quarries near the Bavarian village of Solnhofen. This stone is so fine-grained that, in the same quarries, workers have found some of the most perfect fossils ever discovered, including the feathered dinosaur-bird Archaeopteryx. Senefelder found the stone easy to polish and easy to write on.

Senefelder later wrote his own account of how the breakthrough happened, and it has become a famous tale. As he told it, his mother asked him to write down a list of clothes for the washerwoman, and with no paper handy, he scribbled it on a freshly polished stone using his homemade greasy ink, made from wax, soap and lampblack. Afterwards he wondered what would happen if he etched the rest of the stone away with acid, leaving his writing raised up like type. That is the story he told, and historians usually repeat it as his own memory rather than as checked fact.

His early experiments, starting around 1796, were with raised writing, a kind of relief printing from stone. But over the next couple of years, roughly by 1798, he discovered something much stranger and more powerful. He did not need to carve or etch the stone deeply at all. A completely flat stone could print, using nothing but chemistry. In 1796 he also started a small publishing business with the composer Franz Gleissner, printing sheet music, which turned out to be one of the first big uses of the new method.

sections.heading: The Oil-and-Water Trick
paragraphs: Every printing method before Senefelder worked by shape. In woodblock printing and in Gutenberg's type, the parts that print stand up higher than the rest, so the ink roller only touches them. That is called relief printing. In engraving, the opposite happens: lines are cut into a metal plate, ink is pushed into the grooves, the surface is wiped clean, and paper pressed hard against it pulls the ink out. That is called intaglio printing. Senefelder's method was something new: the printing surface was completely flat. Printers call this planographic printing, meaning printing from a plane, or flat, surface.

How can a flat stone print a picture? The secret is a fact you can see in your own kitchen: oil and water do not mix. Pour a little cooking oil into a glass of water and it floats in blobs, refusing to blend. Water molecules are strongly attracted to each other and pull away from oily molecules, so the two stay separate.

Here is how a lithographer uses this. First, an artist draws on the smooth stone with a greasy crayon or a greasy liquid ink called tusche. The grease soaks a little way into the slightly porous limestone. Next, the printer coats the stone with a solution of gum arabic, a sticky substance from acacia trees, mixed with a weak acid. This treatment makes all the bare areas of the stone love water and hold onto it, while the greasy drawing stays water-repelling.

Now the printing begins. A worker wipes the stone with a wet sponge. Water clings to the bare stone but beads up and runs off the greasy drawing. Then he rolls oily printing ink over the whole surface. The ink sticks to the greasy drawing but is pushed away by the wet stone around it. A sheet of paper is laid on top and the stone and paper are run through a press with a scraping bar. Lift the paper, and there is the drawing, printed. Wet the stone again, ink again, print again: hundreds of copies can be made from one drawing.

Senefelder first called his invention stone printing or chemical printing. The French name, lithographie, won out, and in English it became lithography. The word comes from two Greek words: lithos, meaning stone, and graphein, meaning to write. Lithography literally means stone writing.

Senefelder took out patents in several countries and in 1818 published a thick instruction book on the whole art of stone printing, which was translated into French and English the following year. He died in Munich in 1834. His process had one huge advantage over engraving: an artist could draw directly on the stone in a natural way, with all the soft shading of a crayon drawing, and the printer could reproduce it faithfully. Great artists noticed. Francisco Goya made lithographs of bullfights in the 1820s, Eugène Delacroix illustrated Goethe's Faust, and the French artist Honoré Daumier drew thousands of lithographed cartoons poking fun at politicians for Paris newspapers.

sections.heading: A Rainbow of Stones: Chromolithography
paragraphs: If one stone could print one color, why not use several stones to print many colors? That idea became chromolithography, from the Greek word chroma, meaning color. In July 1837 the French printer Godefroy Engelmann of Mulhouse received a patent for a color lithography method, though some historians argue that colored lithographs were being made a little earlier.

Chromolithography was slow, careful, skilled work. For each color, the artist had to draw a separate stone showing only where that color should go. A yellow stone, a red stone, a blue stone, a stone for skin tones, a stone for shadows, and so on. Each sheet of paper went through the press once for each stone. To make the colors land in exactly the right places, printers used small marks or pins to line up the paper precisely every time, called registration. Using twelve colors was not unusual, and some prints needed many more. One example in the New York Public Library's collection was made with 19 stones.

The results were dazzling. In the 1800s, before color photography, chromolithographs brought bright color to ordinary homes for the first time. Families hung cheap copies of famous paintings, nicknamed chromos, on their walls. Shops sold colorful labels for fruit crates, cigar boxes and tin cans. Children collected trade cards, little advertising pictures given away by stores. Scientists used chromolithographs to show birds, flowers, rocks and the human body in accurate color.

In the United States, a German-born printer named Louis Prang became famous for his chromolithographs. He published color copies of popular paintings and printed the first American Christmas cards, helping start a tradition that still fills mailboxes every December.

Lithography also gave birth to the modern poster. In Paris in the late 1800s, artists such as Jules Chéret and Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec designed huge, brilliantly colored posters for theaters, cabarets, bicycles and drinks. Printed by color lithography, they turned city walls into an open-air art gallery. People even peeled them off walls to collect them.

Heavy stones were eventually replaced by thin, flexible metal plates that could wrap around a cylinder, and chromolithography was replaced by cheaper and faster color printing methods by the late 1930s. But the oil-and-water trick at its heart never went away. Keep that in mind for later in this Deep Dive.

sections.heading: The Slowest Job and Mergenthaler's Answer
paragraphs: By the 1880s, as we saw in the last part, steam-driven rotary presses could print tens of thousands of newspapers an hour. Yet every single letter on every page still had to be picked out of a type case by a human hand. Picture a big-city newspaper composing room at night: rows of men standing at slanted wooden cases, their fingers darting from compartment to compartment, clicking tiny metal letters into composing sticks. A skilled compositor was fast, but even the best could set only a few thousand letters in an hour, and a large newspaper page holds tens of thousands. Then, after printing, every letter had to be sorted back into its little box.

Newspapers grew bigger and bigger, and they needed armies of compositors. Their speed and accuracy often decided how much they were paid. Publishers dreamed of a machine that could set type the way a typist types a letter.

Many inventors tried and failed. Some built machines that picked up ready-made pieces of type and lined them up, but sorting the used type back into place proved terribly difficult. The most famous failure was the Paige Compositor, a marvelously complicated machine with thousands of parts. The author Mark Twain invested a fortune in it over many years and lost it when the machine proved too fragile and fussy to compete. The winning idea came from a different direction: instead of handling old type at all, why not cast fresh type every time?

Ottmar Mergenthaler was born in 1854 in the kingdom of Württemberg in southern Germany. He trained as a watchmaker and clockmaker, a perfect apprenticeship for someone who would one day build a machine with thousands of tiny moving parts. In 1872, at the age of eighteen, he emigrated to the United States and went to work in a relative's instrument workshop, which soon settled in Baltimore, Maryland, making scientific instruments and models for inventors' patents.

In 1876 Mergenthaler was approached by James O. Clephane, a court stenographer (a person who records everything said in a courtroom), and his partners, who wanted a faster way to produce printed copies of legal papers. That project led him to the problem of typesetting. For years he built and abandoned prototypes. By 1884 he had settled on the key idea: the machine would assemble a row of small moulds for an entire line of text, then pour molten metal into them to cast the whole line as one solid bar.

In 1886 he had a working machine and founded a company to make it. A group of newspaper publishers had helped pay for the development, among them Whitelaw Reid, the publisher of the New-York Tribune. So it was in the Tribune's composing room in July 1886 that the first Linotype went to work on a real daily newspaper. The same year, the Tribune used it to set a book, The Tribune Book of Open-Air Sports, the first book ever set on a Linotype.

The name explained the trick: the machine produced a line of type all at once. You will often read that someone in the Tribune office exclaimed that it made a line o' type, giving the machine its name. That is a popular story, but there is no firm record of who said it first, so it is best treated as a legend.

The Tribune was delighted. By 1889 it had 42 Linotypes working at once. Other papers rushed to buy them, and soon the clatter of Linotypes filled composing rooms around the world. Mergenthaler, sadly, did not enjoy his success for long. He clashed with the newspaper investors running the company and was pushed aside. He fell ill with tuberculosis and died in Baltimore in 1899, aged only 45.

sections.heading: Inside a Linotype
paragraphs: A Linotype looks like a cross between a giant typewriter, a pipe organ and a small factory. It stands taller than an adult and has thousands of parts. One early model, the Square Base Linotype, had about 5,000 parts and cost about 1,000 dollars, a large sum at the time. Here is what happens when an operator sits down at it.

The operator faces a keyboard of 90 keys. Above it sits a slanted metal box called the magazine, divided into long channels. Each channel holds a stack of matrices, small flat pieces of brass with the shape of a letter cut into one edge. Remember the matrices from Gutenberg's hand mould? These are the same idea, a mould for a letter, but now hundreds of them are stored inside a machine.

When the operator presses a key, say the letter e, a little gate opens at the bottom of the e channel and one brass matrix drops out. It slides down onto a moving belt and lines up next to the previous letter in a holder called the assembler. When the operator presses the space key, the machine drops in a spaceband instead: two thin wedges of steel sliding against each other.

When the line is almost full, the operator pulls a lever and the machine takes over. The spacebands are pushed upward. Because they are wedge-shaped, they get wider as they rise, spreading the words apart until the line fills exactly the right width. That is justification, the job hand compositors used to do by slipping in tiny spaces one by one, now done in a second.

Next comes the hot part. Behind the line of matrices sits a pot of molten type metal, an alloy mostly of lead with some antimony and tin, kept at about 280 degrees Celsius. A plunger squirts the liquid metal into a mould pressed against the line of matrices. In moments it cools and hardens into a single metal bar with a whole line of raised, backwards letters along its top edge. This bar is called a slug. The machine trims it and drops it onto a tray, next to the slug before it. Line by line, a column of slugs grows into a page.

The cleverest part of all happens last. An arm lifts the used matrices to the top of the machine, onto a long bar called the distributor bar. Every matrix has a pattern of notched teeth along its top, a different pattern for each letter, like a key. As the matrices slide along the bar, each one stays hanging until it reaches the spot where the bar's ridges no longer match its teeth. There it drops neatly into its own channel in the magazine, ready to be used again. The machine sorts its own letters, solving the problem that defeated so many earlier inventors.

A Linotype let one operator set type roughly three to five times faster than a hand compositor. And because every slug was brand new, the letters were always sharp. If the operator made a mistake, though, there was a catch: the whole line had to be cast again. After printing, the slugs were simply melted down and the metal reused.

sections.heading: Monotype: One Letter at a Time, by Paper Tape
paragraphs: At almost the same time, another American inventor had a different idea. Tolbert Lanston was born in 1844 in Troy, Ohio, and later lived in Washington, D.C. In June 1887 he received patents for a typesetting system that came to be called the Monotype, meaning single type.

The Monotype split the job between two separate machines. The first was a keyboard. As the operator typed, the keyboard did not cast anything. Instead, it punched patterns of holes into a long paper tape, a bit like the rolls that play tunes on a player piano. The operator could work in a quiet office far from the hot metal.

The paper tape was then fed into the second machine, the caster. Jets of compressed air passing through the holes told the caster which letter to make next. The caster moved a frame full of matrices so that the right one sat above a mould, squirted in molten metal, and cast a single, separate letter. One by one, the letters were pushed into lines, with exactly the right spaces calculated in advance so every line came out justified.

Why build it this way? Because individual letters are easier to correct. If a word was wrong, a worker could pluck out a single letter with tweezers instead of recasting a whole line. That made the Monotype especially popular for books, scientific works, timetables and complicated tables of numbers, where accuracy and beautiful spacing mattered more than speed. Linotypes ruled newspapers; Monotypes were loved by book printers.

Lanston's company succeeded thanks to many helpers, especially the engineer John Sellers Bancroft, who greatly improved the machine. In Britain, the Monotype Corporation also became famous for typefaces. In 1932 it produced Times New Roman, designed for The Times of London, the same newspaper that had first used Koenig's steam press back in 1814. Some people call that punched paper tape an early step toward digital typesetting, since it stored text as a code of holes that a machine could read.

sections.heading: Pictures Made of Dots
paragraphs: Text was now fast. Pictures were another matter. Photography had been invented in the 1830s, but for decades newspapers could not print photographs at all. The problem is that a printing press puts down ink or no ink, black or white. A photograph is full of smooth grays, from pale silver to deep shadow. How can a press that only prints solid black make gray?

Until the 1880s, the answer was to copy photos by hand. Artists redrew a photograph onto a block of wood, and skilled engravers cut it into a printing block, using clusters of fine lines to suggest shading. Magazines such as Harper's Weekly employed teams of these artists. It worked, but it took time and the engraver's hand always changed the picture a little.

The solution is called the halftone. As early as 1852, the English photography pioneer William Henry Fox Talbot suggested using a fine screen, like a veil, to break an image into tiny pieces for printing. Over the next few decades many inventors experimented with the idea.

On 4 March 1880, the New York Daily Graphic printed a picture called A Scene in Shantytown, New York, showing simple wooden shacks on the edge of the city. It is generally described as the first halftone photograph printed in a newspaper. The Daily Graphic, founded in 1873, was the first American daily newspaper with illustrations every day, and its work on photo printing was led by Stephen Henry Horgan. The 1880 screen was crude and the picture looked rough, but it proved the idea worked.

Better methods quickly followed. In 1882 the German inventor Georg Meisenbach patented a process he called autotype and became the first to make relief halftones a commercial success. In the United States, Frederic Ives and the brothers Louis and Max Levy improved the process by producing high-quality glass screens ruled with crisscrossing lines.

Here is how a halftone works. The photograph is rephotographed through a screen covered with a fine grid of lines. The screen breaks the image into a pattern of dots, all evenly spaced. Where the picture is dark, the dots come out big and almost touch. Where it is light, the dots are tiny specks surrounded by white paper. The press only ever prints solid black dots, but your eye cannot see dots that small from normal reading distance, so it blends them together and sees smooth shades of gray. That is why the result is called a halftone.

You can test this yourself. Take a magnifying glass and look closely at a photograph in a printed newspaper or magazine. You will see the dots. Newspaper screens are fairly coarse, often around 85 lines of dots per inch, because cheap, absorbent newsprint makes ink spread. Glossy magazine paper can hold much finer screens with far more dots, which is why magazine photos look sharper.

sections.heading: Newspapers Explode, and Jobs Change
paragraphs: Put Linotypes, rotary presses, cheap wood-pulp paper and halftone photographs together, and you get the giant newspaper of around 1900. Big-city papers grew to dozens of pages, with special Sunday editions much thicker still. Some printed hundreds of thousands of copies a day. In 1890 the reformer Jacob Riis published How the Other Half Lives, a book about the crowded tenements of New York, and some of his photographs were reproduced as halftones, helping readers see poverty with their own eyes. Photojournalism, telling news with photographs, was born.

Advertising boomed alongside. Department stores bought whole pages to show their goods. Mail-order catalogues full of pictures let families on distant farms shop by post. Color lithography printed eye-catching posters and labels, and cheaper color printing on newspaper presses made something new possible: the color comic strip. In 1895 Richard Outcault's character known as the Yellow Kid began appearing in color in New York's Sunday papers, one of the ancestors of today's comics.

For workers, the new machines brought both loss and opportunity. Hand compositors feared that Linotypes would put them out of work, and in some shops jobs were cut. But newspapers were growing so fast that many compositors retrained as Linotype operators, and printers' unions bargained for better conditions. The productivity of the machines helped compositors win shorter working days, including a nine-hour day. Linotype operating also became a skilled trade that some women and deaf workers entered, since the work depended on sharp eyes and quick fingers rather than hearing.

Hot-metal typesetting ruled for nearly a century. Then computers arrived. In July 1978, The New York Times stopped setting its paper in hot metal and switched to a computer-based system, retiring its last 61 Linotypes. A few working Linotypes still clatter away in museums and small print shops, kept alive by enthusiasts who love the smell of hot metal.
But one invention from this story was about to become more important than ever. Senefelder's oil-and-water trick was about to become the backbone of almost all modern printing.

deepDive: Halftones are a beautiful example of science and perception working together. A printing press is essentially binary: at any point on the paper there is ink or there is not. A halftone fakes continuous tone using a property of human vision called spatial integration. The eye's lens and retina cannot resolve detail finer than about one arcminute at normal viewing distances, so when dots are smaller than that, the brain averages the light reflected from a small area. If 30 percent of a patch is covered with ink, it looks like a 30 percent gray. Halftone screens are described in lines per inch: coarse newsprint often uses around 85, while glossy magazine and book printing commonly use much finer screens. Finer screens give smoother pictures, but tiny dots on absorbent paper spread out and blur, an effect printers call dot gain, so each paper has a practical limit. In the early process, the photograph was rephotographed through a glass screen ruled with crossed lines a short distance in front of the film; optical effects of the screen turned bright areas into large dots and dark areas into small ones on the negative, which became the reverse on the printing plate. Today software does this mathematically. Typesetting machines raise a different debate: who should get credit, and was the Linotype really revolutionary? Mergenthaler's machine succeeded where dozens of earlier composing machines failed largely because it avoided distributing used type: it cast fresh type and melted the old. Yet it relied on the matrix idea that goes back to Gutenberg's hand mould, and its commercial success depended on investors like Whitelaw Reid and the huge market of daily newspapers. Labour historians also argue about its effects. Some compositors lost jobs, but newspaper growth absorbed many of them, and unions negotiated training and hours. Finally, Lanston's Monotype keyboard stored text as punched holes on paper tape, separate from the casting machine. Separating the input of text from its output is the same basic idea used in later phototypesetting and in digital publishing, which is why some historians see the Monotype as an ancestor of computer typesetting.
funFact: The fine-grained limestone from Solnhofen in Bavaria, prized for lithography stones, is the same rock in which fossils of the feathered Archaeopteryx were found, which is why one species is named Archaeopteryx lithographica.

check.q: In a Linotype machine, what is a slug?
check.a: A solid metal bar with a whole line of type cast on it
